title: Soma for the Classroom
author: Mark Fraser
summary: Fraser uses Aldous Huxley's soma -- the drug that removes all discomfort in Brave New World -- as an extended metaphor for frictionless ed-tech, arguing that the desire to remove struggle from learning is often counter-productive because discomfort is where learning actually happens. He distinguishes two mechanisms modern learning tools conflate under the single banner of 'engagement': absorption (keeping a student's attention, often via unpredictable variable-ratio rewards borrowed from slot-machine and social-media design) and friction removal (making a task feel easy). Drawing on B.F. Skinner's own teaching machines, which deliberately avoided variable-ratio rewards in favor of continuous, errorless reinforcement, Fraser argues that modern edtech tools blend both mechanisms together in ways Skinner himself kept separate, producing gamified engagement that looks like learning without reliably producing it. His central test for evaluating any AI tool or task is not whether it is difficult, but whether it removes the productive struggle that creates the learning versus work that was never the point of it -- using a calculator in a mechanics lesson versus an arithmetic lesson as his worked example. He closes by noting that AI breaks the old 'tool test' because, unlike a calculator, it has no fixed edges: what it takes from a learner depends entirely on how it is used in each individual exchange, making the real diagnostic question what the learner handed over to AI, and whether that was the thing they were meant to be learning to do. Found via Sarah Findlater's Weekly Reading Rundown roundup (8.9.26); article's own publication date is July 30, 2026.
points: Fraser distinguishes two mechanisms modern edtech conflates as 'engagement': absorption (keeping attention, often via unpredictable variable-ratio rewards) and friction removal (making tasks feel easy) -- neither alone has anything to do with whether learning occurred.

B.F. Skinner deliberately avoided variable-ratio reinforcement in his own teaching machines, believing classroom learning should be errorless -- but used exactly that method to condition his pigeons, a distinction Fraser says modern edtech no longer respects.

Citing Kim and Castelli's meta-analysis, Fraser notes gamification does produce positive effects but they tend to be short-lived and diminish as novelty fades, because gamification weighs heavily on absorption and lightly on productive friction.

His core diagnostic question for any AI tool or task: does it remove the productive struggle that creates the learning, or work that was never the point of it -- illustrated by a calculator that helps in a mechanics lesson but defeats the purpose in an arithmetic lesson.

Because AI has no fixed 'edges' like a calculator or classic spell-checker, Fraser argues the only reliable question becomes what the learner handed over to AI, and whether that was the thing they were meant to be learning to do.
quotes: In education, things are different. In that domain, the desire to remove friction is often counter-productive because it is in the discomfort that the learning happens.

A reward delivered on an unpredictable schedule, sometimes after one correct response, sometimes after several, produces behaviour far more persistent than a reward every time. This is the variable-ratio schedule.
Significantly, Skinner didn't use variable-ratio schedules in his own teaching machines, believing that classroom learning should be errorless and guided by continuous, immediate reinforcement.
The reason the gains are shallow and temporary is because gamification tends to weigh heavily on the absorption side of the balance and much less on the friction side.
Does it remove the productive struggle that creates the learning, or work that was never the point of it?
What it takes away from the learner is not fixed by what it is; it is decided, exchange by exchange, according to how it is used.
Like Soma, frictionless learning requires us to notice what is missing in the moment and then to insist on retaining the discomfort that keeps us learning because that is what keeps us human.
